slot.brief: Use the scalar triple product/determinant condition to test whether three points or two lines and a point are coplanar, or find the shortest distance between skew lines.

stem: The lines $\mathbf r=(0,0,3)+s(1,2,0)$ and $\mathbf r=(-1,3,2)+t(2,-1,1)$ intersect. If $P=(2,0,k)$ is coplanar with them, find $k$.

verdicts.working: The lines intersect at (1,2,3). Coplanarity requires (1,2,0)×(2,-1,1) · (P−(1,2,3)) = 0, giving 19−5k=0, so k=19/5.

working:
At $s=t=1$, the intersection is $C=(1,2,3)$.
$\vec u=(1,2,0),\quad \vec v=(2,-1,1),\quad \overrightarrow{CP}=(1,-2,k-3)$.
$\vec u	imes\vec v=(2,-1,-5)$.
$\overrightarrow{CP}\cdot(\vec u	imes\vec v)=2+2-5(k-3)=19-5k=0$.
$k=\dfrac{19}{5}$

Independent check: The lines intersect at (1,2,3). Coplanarity requires (1,2,0)×(2,-1,1) · (P−(1,2,3)) = 0, giving 19−5k=0, so k=19/5.
solution:
The lines intersect at $C=(1,2,3)$. Coplanarity requires the scalar triple product to vanish:
$$\bigl((1,2,0)\times(2,-1,1)\bigr)\cdot(1,-2,k-3)=0.$$
Since $(1,2,0)\times(2,-1,1)=(2,-1,-5)$, we get $19-5k=0$, hence $k=\dfrac{19}{5}$.
